title: API 510 Training in Toledo, OH: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 510 exam prep for Toledo, Oregon and Lima vessel inspectors: hydrocracker, reformer and coker vessels, Ohio special inspectors, self-paced online.
h1: API 510 training in Toledo: exam preparation for pressure vessel inspectors at the Oregon and Lima refineries and the plants of north-west Ohio
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors in Toledo and north-west Ohio

Most API 510 work within reach of Toledo sits in four refineries: two just outside the city, one at Lima to the south and one in Detroit to the north. They run columns, hydrocracker and reformer reactors, coke drums, amine vessels and long banks of exchangers. Each has a thickness history and a date by which somebody must decide whether it can run another cycle; making and defending that decision is the API 510 inspector's job.

Atlantis NDT's API 510 course prepares you for the examination. It is self-paced and online: you begin when you enrol, work at the speed your shifts allow and send questions to an instructor who answers from the code text. There is no Atlantis classroom in Toledo; Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and the course runs on its learning portal. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the certification to those who pass.

Four refineries, read through EIA's unit figures

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's 2026 Refinery Capacity Report lists every operable refinery as of the start of the year, unit by unit and under its current owner. For a vessel inspector the downstream columns matter most, because each unit brings its own vessels and damage.

Refinery and ownerCrude distillationSelected downstream units, barrels per stream daySulfur, short tons per day
Toledo Refining Co LLC (PBF Energy), near Toledo172,800 b/cdCatalytic cracking 82,000; distillate hydrocracking 52,000; high-pressure reforming 51,800; aromatics 10,800116
Ohio Refining Company LLC (Cenovus Energy), Oregon, Ohio150,800 b/cdVacuum distillation 72,500; delayed coking 36,000; catalytic cracking 55,000; gas oil hydrocracking 32,500; reforming 42,000; asphalt 9,000462
Lima Refining Company (Cenovus Energy), Lima183,000 b/cdVacuum distillation 57,000; delayed coking 26,100; catalytic cracking 45,300; gas oil hydrocracking 26,000; high-pressure reforming 55,000; aromatics 9,200269
Marathon Petroleum Co LP, Detroit146,000 b/cdVacuum distillation 90,500; delayed coking 40,500; asphalt 32,000435

Read the last column first: sulfur recovery capacity is a fair guide to how much sulfur a crude slate brings in, and the two plants beside Toledo sit far apart on it. PBF says its 282-acre refinery runs light, sweet crudes from Canada, the Mid-continent, the Bakken and the Gulf Coast, and its sulfur capacity is about a quarter of its neighbour's. Cenovus's Oregon refinery, opened in 1919 by the company's account and now making asphalt, coke and sulfur alongside fuels, carries a delayed coker and a large vacuum unit.

Lima, which Cenovus calls the longest-running continuously operating oil refinery in the United States, has run since 1886 and adds coking, hydrocracking and aromatics. Marathon's Detroit refinery, about 60 miles north by PBF's own distance, is a coking refinery with large asphalt capacity. The owner-user inspection groups at these plants, and the contractors who staff their turnarounds, hold most of the full-time API 510 work around Toledo.

What these units put on a Toledo vessel inspector's list

The current API 510 Body of Knowledge examines fifteen damage mechanism paragraphs of API RP 571, plus its definitions, and nothing else from that document. Mapped onto the units in the table, they fall into four groups.

Hydrogen service: hydrocrackers and reformers

Both refineries beside Toledo and Lima run hydrocrackers and reformers, so high-temperature hydrogen attack (RP 571, 3.36) and high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion (3.35) are the mechanisms most likely to drive planning on reactor circuits. HTHA gives little surface warning, so learn what drives it, which steels RP 571 links to it and why finding it is specialist work. Reformers carry a second trap: chlorides from the catalyst and its regeneration can cause hydrochloric acid corrosion (3.37) in effluent and stabiliser equipment, not only in the crude overhead where most people expect HCl.

Sour service: amine, sour water and the coker

Where sulfur capacity is high, so is the count of vessels in wet H2S service: amine contactors and regenerators, sour water strippers, fractionator overhead drums. Wet H2S damage (3.67) in its blistering, HIC, SOHIC and SSC forms and amine stress corrosion cracking (3.3) belong here, with sulfidation (3.61) in hot crude, vacuum and coker sections. Naphthenic acid corrosion (3.46) matters or not depending on the crudes a site buys.

Water, steam and caustic

Deaerators, condensate drums and blowdown vessels in the steam system bring boiler water and steam condensate corrosion (3.9). Caustic corrosion and caustic cracking (3.14 and 3.15) follow caustic treating, and chloride stress corrosion cracking (3.17) affects austenitic stainless shells, internals and tubing.

Weather, insulation and flow

Lake Erie winters make brittle fracture (3.11) practical on thick vessels started cold or hydrotested in winter, and freeze-thaw cycling drives corrosion under insulation (3.22) and atmospheric corrosion (3.8). Erosion and erosion-corrosion (3.27) complete the fifteen.

Temper embrittlement of chrome-moly hydroprocessing reactors and polythionic acid cracking of stainless equipment at shutdown are real concerns on these units, yet neither is among the paragraphs the current Body of Knowledge names. Treat them as job knowledge, and check the list for your own window, because API revises it.

Exchangers, steam drums and deaerators: where API 510 meets Ohio's boiler rules

Ohio regulates boilers and pressure vessels through two sets of rules. The Board of Building Standards writes the rules for construction, installation, repair and operation in Ohio Administrative Code chapters 4101:4-1 to 4101:4-10, and rule 4101:4-2-01 says in-service inspections are carried out by general and special inspectors under rules the superintendent of the Division of Industrial Compliance adopts in chapter 1301:3-5. That chapter, within the Ohio Department of Commerce, is built around boilers: power boilers are inspected at intervals of not more than one year and process boilers not more than three, and under Revised Code section 4104.15 the superintendent issues the certificate of operation once the owner or user complies.

A general inspector is a State of Ohio employee. A special inspector holds a National Board commission and an Ohio commission and usually works for an insurer, but the definition in rule 4101:4-1-01 also lets an owner-user employ one, provided the owner-user maintains an inspection programme meeting the National Board's NB-371 rules for owner-user inspection organisations; while acting as a special inspector, that person represents the state and acts independently of the employer. An API 510 certificate is not an Ohio commission and replaces nothing in that system, though some inspectors in owner-user programmes hold both.

The same definitions name categories older plants still meet. An "Ohio-standard" vessel was built to the former Ohio industrial commission rules but never ASME-stamped, an "Ohio special" was approved by special action of the Board although it does not fully comply with ASME, and a "non-standard" vessel was installed before July 1913 without stamping to Ohio rules. None of this is exam material, but it explains a nameplate that does not look the way the textbook says it should.

Exchangers deserve their own note. ASME PCC-2 Article 312, on inspection and repair of shell-and-tube heat exchangers, is examined alongside API RP 572 on vessel inspection practice, while the tubesheet calculations of Section VIII Part UHX are excluded. Expect questions on inspection, plugging and repair rather than design. Background reading: heat exchanger tube inspection methods.

Worked example: an ellipsoidal head, the next interval and MAWP for the next run

Head questions cost marks because the interval and MAWP rules interlock. Take a hydrotreater separator with 2:1 ellipsoidal heads, 72 in. inside diameter, designed for 250 psig; the problem gives S = 20,000 psi and E = 1.0 for a seamless head, with no static head.

  1. Required thickness of a 2:1 ellipsoidal head under UG-32: t = PD ÷ (2SE − 0.2P) = (250 × 72) ÷ (40,000 − 50) = 18,000 ÷ 39,950 = 0.451 in.
  2. Readings at the head knuckle CML: 0.625 in. sixteen years ago, 0.595 in. eight years ago and 0.535 in. today. Long-term rate = 0.090 ÷ 16 = 0.0056 in. per year; short-term rate = 0.060 ÷ 8 = 0.0075 in. per year. The faster short-term rate followed a feed change and reflects current conditions, so it governs.
  3. Remaining corrosion allowance = 0.535 − 0.451 = 0.084 in., and remaining life = 0.084 ÷ 0.0075 = 11.3 years.
  4. Internal or on-stream interval: the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years, which gives 5.6 years.
  5. MAWP for continued service: API 510 uses the measured thickness minus twice the corrosion expected before the next inspection. For a five-year run: 0.535 − 2 × (0.0075 × 5) = 0.460 in., and P = 2SEt ÷ (D + 0.2t) = 18,400 ÷ 72.09 = 255 psi, above the 250 psig design.

Now run the same numbers over the full 5.6 years. The thickness used becomes 0.535 − 2 × 0.042 = 0.451 in., the required thickness again, and the MAWP comes out at 250 psi exactly. That is no coincidence: twice the loss over half the remaining life is the whole remaining corrosion allowance, so the two rules meet at the same point. The trap sits on the other side: use the slower long-term rate and the remaining life stretches to 15 years and the interval to 7.5, a tidy option that hides a vessel now losing metal faster. See also the API 510 code explainer.

Who sits API 510 around Toledo, and how the experience adds up

API counts education plus vessel experience from the last ten years, gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, owner-user inspection groups included. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year supervising or performing inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years, one of them in inspection; a high school diploma needs three; no formal education needs five or more. The API 510 certification requirements page has the detail. Local candidates usually arrive by one of four routes.

  • NDT technicians. Thickness gaugers on refinery contracts build vessel experience quickly; the inspection year accrues once they evaluate readings rather than only take them. NDT training in Toledo covers the ASNT SNT-TC-1A route into that work.
  • Welders and boilermakers. Owens Community College offers a welding associate degree and a pipe welding certificate. Fabrication and repair years count towards the total; whether an associate degree counts as engineering or technology education is API's decision.
  • Operators. Operating years count towards the longer routes, but the inspection year has to be earned in an inspection role.
  • Engineers. The University of Toledo requires its engineering science students to complete three semester-long paid co-ops, starting in the second year. A placement in a refinery inspection group is a strong start, though API decides whether co-op time counts.

Three or more years of technical military service count like a bachelor's degree unless the discharge was dishonorable. Log the vessels and tasks you work on, because API verifies documented experience.

Studying for API 510 around Oregon and Lima turnarounds

Refinery work around Toledo follows turnarounds and a winter that slows outdoor jobs. Self-paced study fits that pattern: stop for the weeks of twelve-hour turnaround shifts, then resume where the portal left you. A sequence that works for many:

  1. API 510 first, learning the interval, corrosion rate and remaining life rules well enough to work without the book, since the Body of Knowledge says those formulas may be closed-book.
  2. Section VIII by the Body of Knowledge list: UG-27 and UG-32, joint efficiency from UW-11 and UW-12, static head, UG-99 and UG-100 test pressure, UCS-66 impact exemption and weld sizes at openings.
  3. RP 571 mapped onto your own unit, finding one real vessel for each of the fifteen paragraphs so you can picture it in the closed-book half.
  4. Section IX and RP 577, reviewing a WPS against its PQR until checking variables becomes routine, then timed papers that copy the real split.

Bring job questions too, such as a nameplate radiography marking you cannot read or a rerate letter in an old file; the instructor answers from the code text, so you learn where each answer lives.

Sitting the API 510 exam from Toledo

API 510 is taken in person on a single day, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Toledo; book once API has accepted your application. The day runs to 7.5 hours: a short tutorial, 110 closed-book questions in 2.75 hours, a 45-minute lunch break, then 60 open-book questions in 3.75 hours. Of the 170 questions, 140 are scored. In the open-book half the codes are PDFs on screen; papers, notes and books stay outside. Windows and their application deadlines are on the API exam schedule page.

Ways to prepare from Toledo, compared

Intensive seminars before exam windows, in person elsewhere or online at fixed times, suit candidates who already know the codes and can be released for the dates. Mentoring inside an owner-user group teaches site procedures and software, though not always open-book technique. Self-paced online study with instructor Q&A, the Atlantis format, suits rotating shifts and anyone who needs to repeat the calculations before they stick. With any of them, check that the material follows your window's Publications Effectivity Sheet and that the practice questions are original. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider; the certificate comes only from passing API's examination.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Toledo-area plant or contractor

Owner-users and inspection contractors around Toledo often prepare several people at once, for example before a contract that names API 510 inspectors. A single enquiry covers the whole group, and fees are quoted on request. Eligibility stays personal: confirm each person's documented vessel experience before enrolling them, because every candidate applies to API and sits the exam alone. In the United States Atlantis performs UT, MT, PT and VT inspection and does not perform radiography; ultrasonic testing in Toledo describes that side of its work.

faq.q: Can I attend an API 510 class in person in Toledo?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in the Toledo area, and the API 510 course is studied online at your own pace with an instructor answering your questions. Other providers run fixed-date seminars. However you prepare, the examination itself is sat in person at a Prometric test centre.

faq.q: Does an Ohio special inspector commission replace API 510, or the other way round?
faq.a: Neither replaces the other. An Ohio special inspector holds National Board and Ohio commissions and makes the inspections state rules require, for an insurer or for an owner-user running an NB-371 programme. API 510 is a private certification refinery owner-users ask for in their own vessel programmes.

faq.q: Are deaerators and condensate drums part of API 510 work at a Toledo refinery?
faq.a: Usually, because deaerators, condensate drums and blowdown vessels are unfired pressure vessels, and boiler water and steam condensate corrosion (RP 571, 3.9) is on the current Body of Knowledge. The boilers themselves, steam drums included, are inspected by a general or special inspector under Ohio's boiler rules.

faq.q: Is temper embrittlement on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Not in the current Body of Knowledge. It lists fifteen RP 571 paragraphs, including high-temperature hydrogen attack, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion, wet H2S damage and brittle fracture, but temper embrittlement is not one of them. It still matters on the chrome-moly reactors of Toledo-area hydrocrackers, so learn it for the job, and check the list again when you book a window.

faq.q: I study engineering at the University of Toledo. Can my co-op count towards API 510?
faq.a: Possibly, but API decides. Its rules count pressure vessel experience gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection group, and with a bachelor's degree you need one year of supervising or performing inspection. Keep a detailed log of any co-op inspection work and present it on your application.

faq.q: Can a Toledo-area inspection contractor enrol several API 510 candidates together?
faq.a: Yes. Tell us how many vessel inspectors you want to prepare and which windows they have in mind, and one quote covers them all. Everyone works through the material on their own schedule with the same instructor access, then makes a personal application to API. Review each person's experience record before enrolling, since API judges eligibility one candidate at a time.
